summary: An implementation report for the ForCES protocol, recording how it was implemented and tested for interoperability against the requirements (RFC 3654) and framework (RFC 3746). It is informational.

eli5.summary: This is a report card showing that different teams built ForCES and got their versions to work with each other.

questions: what is a forces control element
what is a logical functional block
subtitle: A report card showing that independent ForCES implementations could talk to each other in a July 2009 interop test.

tldr.problem: A protocol can only advance if people show that independent implementations of it exist and work together. ForCES, which separates the control plane of a network device from its forwarding plane, needed that evidence for its protocol, model and SCTP transport documents.
tldr.mechanism: The authors surveyed three implementations with a questionnaire and ran an interoperability test in July 2009 in which the implementations exchanged ForCES messages while two extended protocol analyzers checked them.
tldr.outcome: All scenarios were tested successfully and the implementations were found to be interoperable. Most problems were code bugs, fixed mostly on site. Security features, including IPsec, were not tested.

today: RFC 6053 is an Informational document that has been updated by RFC 6984. It is a snapshot of the state of ForCES implementations at the time of publication in November 2010.

sections.title: Why an Implementation Report
sections.content:
This document is an implementation report for the Forwarding and Control Element Separation (ForCES) protocol, the ForCES model and the SCTP-based Transport Mapping Layer (SCTP TML). It follows the outline suggested by RFC 5657 and includes an interoperability report.

ForCES defines an architectural framework and protocols for exchanging information between the control plane and the forwarding plane of a ForCES network element. The requirements are in RFC 3654 and the framework is in RFC 3746. The protocol itself is in RFC 5810, the model in RFC 5812 and the SCTP TML in RFC 5811.

The protocol works in a master-slave mode: forwarding elements (FEs) are slaves and control elements (CEs) are masters. The TML carries the protocol messages and handles transport-level matters such as reliability, congestion control, multicast and ordering. All implementations MUST implement the SCTP TML.
sections.eli5: Some machines are the bosses and some are the workers who follow orders. This report checks that bosses and workers built by different teams understand each other.

sections.title: The Moving Parts of ForCES
sections.content:
The report repeats the terms from RFC 3654 and RFC 3746. A Control Element (CE) runs control and signaling protocols and instructs one or more FEs how to process packets. A Forwarding Element (FE) uses the underlying hardware to do per-packet processing as directed by the CEs.

The basic building block is the Logical Functional Block (LFB), a well-defined block that lives in an FE and is controlled by the CE. LFBs are grouped into classes, identified by an LFB Class ID, and an LFB Instance ID tells apart several instances of one class. LFB components are the flags, arguments and tables that the CE can read or write.

The ForCES protocol here means the Fp reference point between CE and FE. It does not cover CE-to-CE or FE-to-FE communication.
sections.eli5: The boss is the CE, the worker is the FE, and the little tasks a worker knows how to do are the building blocks, called LFBs.

sections.title: The Implementation Survey
sections.content:
Three independent implementations were surveyed with a questionnaire: NTT Japan, the University of Patras and Zhejiang Gongshang University. For each feature, the respondents said whether they had implemented it, would implement it, or would not implement it at all. Extensions to two protocol analyzers, Ethereal/Wireshark and tcpdump, count as implementations too, because they can decode and validate ForCES messages.

The survey found that the three already implemented all the major features. The tables cover protocol messages, main header flags, TLVs, operation types, advanced features, model data types, the FE Protocol and FE Object LFBs, the SCTP priority ports and message handling per priority. Many cells say Will Implement, and all organizations said they intended to implement the outstanding features. This varies because the organizations implement different LFBs.

For the TML security feature, IPsec, all three answered Will Implement. None had implemented it.
sections.eli5: The authors handed out a checklist and asked each team which jobs their machine could already do and which they would add later.

sections.title: The Interoperability Test
sections.content:
The test took place in July 2009 at the University of Patras. The NTT and Patras implementations were there in person, while the Zhejiang Gongshang implementation, which sat behind a NAT, connected remotely from China. Mojatatu Networks and Hangzhou Baud Information and Networks Technology Corporation took part with their extended analyzers, making five independent organizations in total.

The goal was to validate basic protocol functionality, mainly message exchange and handling, so the test parameters were limited. For example, only FULLDATA-TLVs were used, there were no transaction operations, and each message carried at most one LFBSelect-TLV, OPER-TLV and PATH-DATA-TLV.

Seven scenarios were run: pre-association setup, TML priority channel connection, association setup, a CE query, heartbeat monitoring, a simple Config command and association teardown. Teardown was tried three ways: a normal Association Teardown message, stopping heartbeats, and shutting down or rebooting an FE or CE. In the Config scenario, the CE set the FE Heartbeat Policy (FEHBPolicy) to 1 to make the FE send heartbeats, and then changed the heartbeat interval (FEHI).
sections.eli5: Teams from far apart met, some in a room and some over the internet, and played a short game of questions and answers between their machines, from saying hello to saying goodbye.

sections.title: Results and Issues Found
sections.content:
Everything that was tested passed: all implementations handled the tested protocol messages, header flags, TLVs, operations, model types and LFB components, and the analyzers captured them. Batching was not planned but was tried when the test went well, and two implementations handled it. All implementations opened and connected to all three SCTP priority ports.

The report lists ten issues. Most were code bugs fixed on site, such as a deadlock after a Teardown message, TLV padding wrongly counted in the TLV length, and a CE that crashed on unknown LFB selector values. Two were network or SCTP matters: the remote link between China and Greece lost an Association Setup message until it was retransmitted, and heartbeat packets were retransmitted until the SCTP-PR option was used. One ambiguity in the SCTP TML draft about messages sent on the wrong priority channel was fixed by making the message-to-channel mapping a MUST in RFC 5811 before it was published.

At the time of the test the three SCTP priority ports were 6700, 6701 and 6702. RFC 5811 defines 6704, 6705 and 6706. The report says this change does not invalidate the results.
sections.eli5: Almost everything worked. A few mistakes in the programs were found and fixed on the spot, which is exactly why you run a test like this.

sections.title: What Was Not Tested: Security
sections.content:
No security elements of the protocol or the SCTP TML were tested. The survey indicated that none were implemented, though all participants said they intended to. The mandated TML security requirement, IPsec, was not validated and the report does not discuss it. The authors argue that because IPsec is well known and widely deployed, testing without it does not invalidate the tests that were done.

For the actual security considerations of the ForCES protocol and the SCTP TML, the report points to RFC 5810 and RFC 5811.
sections.eli5: The test checked that the machines could talk, but it did not check the lock on the door. The teams said they would add the lock later.
